chapters.title: Chapter 22. The Five on a Screen.
Chapter 24. The Cohort in Tarpon Springs.
Chapter 33. The Painted Table at Sunrise.

spans.text: The Olympic Air flight from Athens to Kos landed at twelve forty-two on the twenty-second of August. The Aegean below the wing had been the most blue water she had ever crossed, and she had not yet found a Sfax-Greek word for the shade of it.
Lina had been on Olympic since five forty.
She had been on Tunisair from Tunis to Athens since two ten Tunis time.
She had been at the Tunis-Carthage gate since ten the night before with her father.
Her father at ten fifteen, in Arabic: bnaytiy.
Baba, she said.
Pothia is the work. Sfax is the kitchen. The work is the work. The kitchen will be here.
Yes, Baba.
Je serai à l’aéroport en juin, he said in French.
I will be here in June, she answered.
He walked her to the security line at one thirty. He kissed her at her forehead. bnaytiy mou.
Baba.
He walked away. He did not turn at the security line. She counted twenty-three steps before he reached the black mat at the swinging doors. She counted nine more after he had passed through.
She walked into security.
The Athens layover had been six hours.

She spent them at the airport gate café with her grandmother Photini’s letter. The letter ran two pages in Sfax-Greek. Photini had given it to her at the painted table on Rue de l’Algérie three days before.
Read at Athens, her grandmother had said. And then put in the bag.
Yes, Yiayia Photini.
She opened the letter at seven in the morning. She read for thirty-four minutes. She did not cry. She closed it and put it in the Moleskine in the front pocket of her backpack.
The Moleskine was her mother’s gift, ruled at the first page in pencil. Three columns: Greek, French, Arabic-by-Latin-letters.
At the last family dinner she had begun the notebook with one entry:
ftáno / j’arrive / anā wāṣila.
I arrive.
She drank her coffee. She counted: fourteen chairs at the café, nine windows in the departure hall, four ground-staff at the gate.
She boarded the Olympic flight at twelve oh five.
Kos to Mastichari. Bus to ferry. Forty-minute hydrofoil. The ferry pulled into Pothia harbor at three oh five.
She counted forty-three passengers as they disembarked. She was the forty-second.

The harbor at three oh five on the twenty-second of August: Mediterranean late-summer dry heat at the dock, sponge boats at the north side, Pothia town rising at the back of the harbor toward the Castle. Three kafenia at the north of the dock. The ferry-office building at the south. At the east end of the dock, a group of program-cohort-locals.
She walked toward the group.
At the front: a short young man in a clean white shirt, twenty-three or twenty-four, dark trousers and leather shoes. He held a placard:
BELHADJ-KOSMA MARIGOULA / VOUVALIS / DROSOS housing Year 1, Cohort B.
She walked to him.
In Greek: I am Lina Belhadj-Kosma.
In Greek: Welcome to Pothia. I am Stelios Vouvalis.
Stelios.
The program office has briefed us. We are at the Drosos house at Vouvalis Street. Four-minute walk.
He took her suitcase. She kept the backpack.

The Pothia streets between dock and Drosos house had whitewashed walls, painted blue shutters, bougainvillea at the front fences, late-summer heat at four oh in the afternoon. Lina counted: four streets walked, eleven painted blue shutters along the fourth street, two kafenia passed.
Stelios said at the third street: You are the fourth.
The fourth.
Phaedon Trakas arrived on the sixteenth. Tia Theodorakis on the eighteenth. Niko Lekkas on the twentieth. You are the fourth.
Athena.
Athena Markou arrives on the twenty-fourth from Tarpon Springs.
He described the dorm before they reached it. Painted blue door at the front courtyard. Olive tree at the north corner. Bougainvillea along the south wall.
She counted the streets and the shutters and the kafenia. She did not count Stelios’s words.
The Drosos house at Vouvalis Street at four oh five had its painted blue door at the front of the courtyard. An old olive tree at the north corner. Bougainvillea along the south wall.
Stelios knocked once.
The woman who opened the door was eighty-two. White hair tied at the back with a white silk ribbon. Grey housedress. Grey cardigan.
Lina Belhadj-Kosma.
Yiayia Marigoula.
Welcome to Pothia. Come in.
The front hall held three things, by Lina’s count: a framed photograph of the 1947 Pothia parish festival on the left wall, an icon of the Theotokos on the right, a wooden hat-rack at the far end.
Yiayia Marigoula walked her through to the dining room at the back: long wooden table, six chairs, sideboard, a framed 1968 Drosos-wedding photograph on the wall above.
Two young men were at the table. They stood.
Phaedon. Niko. This is Lina Belhadj-Kosma from Sfax.
Lina.
Phaedon.
Lina.
Niko.

Phaedon was the taller, fine fingers and dark eyes, a calm at the mouth. Niko was shorter, dark hair, a quiet at the posture. Phaedon held out his hand. They shook. Niko did not. He nodded across the table; she nodded back.

Lina had read the program brief on the five at the Athens layover. Niko at the brief had been the Darwin Greek-Australian, the quiet. The Niko in the Drosos dining room at four ten was the quiet the brief had described.
Sit, Lina mou, said Yiayia Marigoula.
She sat on the east side. Phaedon on the west. Niko on the north. Yiayia Marigoula poured a Greek coffee. Lina took the cup, set it in front of her.

The house has four upstairs bedrooms. Tia and Athena at the east. You in the second east room. Phaedon and Niko at the west. Bathrooms at the middle of the hall, kitchen at the back of the ground floor.
Thank you, Yiayia Marigoula.
The Drosos house has been at Vouvalis Street since the 1882 build. We have had the cohort here since 2008.
Yes.
The kitchen is the kitchen.
The kitchen is the kitchen.
Drink.
She drank. The coffee was strong. It was the kind of strong her grandmother made at the painted table at six in the morning. She set the cup down.
Yiayia Marigoula. Thank you.
Lina mou. The Sfax-Greek.
The Sfax-Greek.

I have known three Sfax-Greek women across my eighty-two years. The first at the Athens parish in 1958 at a Drosos cousin’s wedding. The second at the Pothia parish in 1973 at a visit. The third at the Athens parish in 2002 at a cousin’s funeral.
Yes.
Those three women carried the Sfax-Greek register your grandmother Photini still has at her kitchen. You have her register. The Pothia-Greek register will come. The two are not the same Greek.
The two are not the same Greek.
They are at the same family of Greek.
Yes, Yiayia.
She stood at the head of the table. Stelios will show you upstairs.
The second east bedroom at the top of the stairs was a square room. Single bed at the wall. Wooden desk at the window. Wardrobe. Bedside table with a lamp.
The window looked out at the back courtyard. A lemon tree at the back corner.

Stelios set the suitcase on the floor. Bathroom is the first door at the middle of the hall. Dinner at seven in the kitchen. Yiayia Marigoula cooks. The kind of dinner this house has when the first three cohort-members are at the house. I will be there.
Thank you, Stelios.

Wifi password Vouvalis2026, router in the front hall. Yiayia Photini at Rue de l’Algérie will be at the painted table at five your Athens time. Sfax is an hour behind. Five fifty Pothia time for the call. I will be in the courtyard.
He closed the door behind him.

She stood at the centre of the room and counted: single bed, wooden desk, wardrobe, bedside table, lamp, wall mirror, the framed Drosos-1968 wedding on the left wall, the icon of Saint Nicholas on the right.
Eight.
She sat on the bed, set her backpack on the floor, unzipped the front pocket, and took out the Moleskine. She turned to the first page and added a fourth entry:
pháno / j’arrive enfin / anā wāṣila akhīran.
I arrive at last.

She unpacked. The suitcase held four months of clothes for the run to Christmas, the five books her father had insisted she bring, the framed photograph of Photini at the painted table that her mother had wrapped in a dishcloth, and the enameled brooch her great-grandmother had worn at the Sfax wedding in 1923.

She set the framed photograph on the bedside table. She set the brooch at the corner of the wooden desk. She set the five books on the shelf above the desk. She set the clothes in the wardrobe. She set her toiletries on the bathroom counter.
She came back at five thirty. She sat at the wooden desk. She opened the laptop. She connected to Vouvalis2026. She called her grandmother at five forty.
Photini at eighty-one had her white hair tied at the back with the same white silk ribbon Yiayia Marigoula had worn at the Drosos door. Lina noted the ribbon. She would think about the ribbon later.
Lina mou.
Yiayia.
Pothia.
Pothia. The Drosos house. Yiayia Marigoula. Stelios Vouvalis. Phaedon Trakas. Niko Lekkas.
The four names.
The four names.
Marigoula Drosos was at the Athens parish in 1973 at a Sfax-Greek visit my mother and I made together.
I had not known.
I had not told.
All right.

The visit was a five-day stay at the Cathedral of the Annunciation in May of 1973. Marigoula was twenty-nine. She asked my mother whether the Kosma family at Sfax had a letter from a Sfax girl at Pothia in 1903. My mother said yes. The letter was at the painted table.
Yes.

Marigoula in 1973 was the Drosos house’s organizer. She had been at the storage room since 1969. She said to my mother that the storage room held letters from the Sfax-Pothia sister-relationship across the 1880s through the 1960s, but missing the return-trip. The return-trip letters were at the Sfax kitchens. She asked my mother to send some.
Yes.
My mother sent twelve letters from the Kosma kitchen to the Drosos storage room across 1974 to 1986.
I had not known.
I had not told.
Yes, Yiayia.

Marigoula in 1973 said: the letters at the Drosos storage room are the kind a Sfax-Greek granddaughter of the Kosma kitchen would find at the future at the Pothia program. I had not known then that I would have a granddaughter at the future at the Pothia program. I had a daughter Nora at four.
Mama at four.
Marigoula twenty-nine. I twenty-eight. My mother fifty-one. Nora four.
The four ages.
The four ages.
Photini drank coffee at her painted table and set the cup down.
Lina mou.
Yiayia.

The letter I gave you at the kitchen three days ago. The one you read at Athens. It is from the 1903 sender. Your great-grandmother’s mother’s sister. She was eleven when she was sent to the Pothia household. The letter you read is the first of fifteen the eleven-year-old wrote to her mother at the Sfax kitchen between July 1903 and November 1906. The fifteen are at the painted table, in the drawer my mother kept.
Yes.

The replies are at the Drosos storage room. The fifteen letters my great-grandmother wrote from the Sfax kitchen to her daughter at Pothia across the same three and a half years. Marigoula told my mother in 1973 the Drosos house had kept them since the 1906 final return.
The 1906 final return.
The sender came back to Sfax at fourteen. Married at sixteen in 1908. Three children. Died at sixty-two in Sfax in 1957. Buried at the parish cemetery.
Yes, Yiayia.
Lina mou.
Yes.
The storage room. The replies. You at the storage room at your time. Not the first week. The fifth or sixth, when you have Pothia at the back of your chair and Sfax at the back of your chair both.
Yes.
Marigoula has a chore-errand at her protocol. She will set a broom at the back of the kitchen at the fifth or sixth week. You will go to the storage room for the broom. You will find the replies.
Yes.
You will not tell the house at the finding. You will call me. You will translate. The translation is yours.
The translation is mine.
All right.
They drank. They sat at the video call for a while.
At six fifteen Photini said: Lina mou. The painted table at Sfax has your chair at the back. Through the year. The painted table is the painted table.
The painted table is the painted table.
Go to dinner. I love you.
I love you, Yiayia.
The call ended at six twenty.
She sat at the desk for a while. She opened the Moleskine and added four entries:
ī apokrísis / les réponses / ar-rudūd. The replies.
to katastēma / la pièce de stockage / ghurfat at-takhzīn. The storage room.
pénte i éxi evdomádes / cinq ou six semaines / khamsa aw sitta asābīʿ. Five or six weeks.
to skoupárion / le balai / al-miknasa. The broom.
She closed the notebook and set it on the bedside table next to the photograph.

She sat on the bed for five minutes. She did not yet know that the broom at the back of the kitchen would set itself in her hand the first Friday in October. She did not need to know. She stood. She walked down to the kitchen.
The kitchen at six fifty had Yiayia Marigoula at the stove, Stelios at the back porch, Phaedon at the table with a book, Niko at the back of the kitchen with a tea.
Lina mou. Dinner at seven.
Yes.
Phaedon looked up. Lina. The call.
Yes.
The call to Sfax. The painted table.
The painted table.
All right.
Niko did not speak. He nodded from the back of the kitchen. She nodded back.
She sat on the east side. Yiayia Marigoula brought yiouvarlakia and lemon-greens. The dinner ran seven to eight thirty. Five at the table: Yiayia Marigoula, Stelios, Phaedon, Niko, Lina. They talked.
Stelios told about the Pothia harbor.
Yiayia Marigoula told about the panigyri at Vathy on the eighteenth of October.
Phaedon told about the Trakas piano Yiayia Marigoula had shown him at the Drosos front room on the sixteenth, the first day.
Niko told about the Argyrou yard and the harbor master.
Lina told about late-summer dry heat in Sfax and the painted table at Rue de l’Algérie.
No one talked about the storage room. No one talked about the replies.

Lina counted: five spoons at the table; six chairs around it, one empty for Athena on Monday; three Phaedon-said-Trakas; one Niko-said-the bench; four Yiayia-Marigoula-said-the kitchen; seven Stelios-said-Pothia. She did not count her own words.

The dinner ended at eight thirty. They washed dishes. Yiayia Marigoula went to her flat at the back at nine. Stelios to his parents’ house at the block over at nine fifteen. Phaedon to his room at nine thirty. Niko to the back porch with a tea at nine forty.
Lina sat in the kitchen alone for five minutes. She drank a glass of water. She walked up to her room.
At the wooden desk she opened the Moleskine and added one more entry on the first page:
ī próti méra / le premier jour / al-yawm al-awwal.
The first day.
She set the notebook on the bedside table. She turned off the lamp at ten forty.

Pothia at ten forty on the twenty-second of August 2026 had the late-summer Mediterranean warm at the open window, the smell of the lemon tree at the back corner of the courtyard, the sound of the harbor at a distance.
She lay on her back. The painted table at Rue de l’Algérie. The fifteen letters in the drawer. The replies at the storage room. Five or six weeks.
She closed her eyes. She slept seven hours and forty minutes. She woke at six twenty on the twenty-third of August.

The Pothia at six twenty on the twenty-third of August 2026 had the late-summer Aegean dawn at the east-facing window of the second east bedroom at the Drosos house. The first sliver of light at the east horizon over the port. The smell of the lemon tree at the back-corner. The harbor at the distance.

She lay at the bed for two minutes. She thought of the Tunis-Carthage-gate at ten the night before with her father. Of the Olympic-Air at twelve forty-two. Of the Pothia-ferry-dock at three oh five. Of Stelios-Vouvalis at the placard. Of Yiayia Marigoula at the painted-blue-door. Of Phaedon and Niko at the dining-table. Of Yiayia Photini at the painted-table-Sfax-side at the call. Of the eight-objects at the second-east-bedroom. Of the Moleskine at the bedside table.
She held the eight pictures at the back of her head as a single shape. The shape was the first-day’s. The shape would be the back-of-the-chair-of-the-second-day.
She stood at six twenty-two. She walked to the bedside table. She picked up the Moleskine. She opened it at the second page. She wrote:
ī defteri méra / le deuxième jour / al-yawm ath-thānī. The second day.

She closed the notebook. She set it on the bedside table. She walked to the wooden desk. She picked up the enameled brooch at the corner. She put it in the front trouser pocket of her clean linen shirt at the chair at the foot of the bed.
She walked downstairs to the kitchen at six thirty-five.
Yiayia Marigoula was at the briki on the stove.
Lina mou.
Yiayia Marigoula.
The second day.
The second day.
Yiayia Marigoula poured a Greek coffee.
Year 1 had begun.
